transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-07-15 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~85 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Marta Ivanov (Redwood SE), Evan Cho (Redwood Product), Carlos Mendez (Zenith CTO), Priya Rao (Zenith ML Infra), Liam O'Connor (Zenith Security), Dana Kim (Zenith SRE), Rashid Alvi (Zenith DS)

Summary:
Quick workshop to align on benchmark methodology for Zenith's inference pilot. Focus areas: realistic loadgen (trace-driven vs synthetic), prompt set curation, apples-to-apples comparisons across quantized and unquantized models, KV/prefix cache behavior with multi-user tenancy, and VPC/on-prem constraints for private deployment.

Topics Covered:
- Metrics & measurement (p50/p95/p99 latency, tail, tokens/s, cost-per-1k-tokens)
- Load generation: replaying traces, shaping synthetic traffic, warmup and cold-starts
- Prompt sets: canonicalization, variable length profiles, deterministic seeds
- KV cache: prefix caching, hit-rate measurement, cache priming strategies
- Batching: dynamic vs fixed batching policies, latency SLOs tradeoffs
- Quantization: 8-bit vs 4-bit, quality regressions detection, eval prompts
- VPC/on-prem: network egress, KMS/HSM implications, audit logging capture

00:00:00 Samira: All right everyone, thanks for making time. We thought we would run through a hands-on methodology so we can get concrete runs that match Zenith's traffic. Quick intro from Redwood side, jordan and marta will lead the loadgen and kv topics.
00:00:15 Carlos: Thanks, yeah we want apples to apples, sorry i keep saying apples but you know what i mean — comparable runs so our procurement and security teams are comfortable.
00:00:30 Jordan: Totally. We'll start with the measurement matrix — what we measure and how. For example p50/p95/p99 at token-level and request-level, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and also cost modeled per 1M tokens.
00:00:45 Priya: Important to call out sequence length distributions. Our production prompts have heavy tail — 80% under 256 tokens but 5% exceed 1024. How do we simulate that?
00:01:05 Marta: We recommend replaying a 48-hour trace as priority one. If you can't share raw data, export length histogram + representative sample prompts and we'll generate synthetic traces that preserve the distribution.
00:01:35 Liam: On the security front, what data leaves our VPC during the test? We need to prove PII is never exfil.
00:01:50 Samira: Good question. For on-prem and VPC private deployments, the control plane can be air-gapped; telemetry can be filtered. We'll include a security checklist in the artifacts.
00:02:10 Rashid: For the prompt sets, should we canonicalize templates? We have many prompts with similar scaffolding — templates plus injected patient data.
00:02:25 Jordan: Yes canonicalization helps. We'll provide a prompt-sanitization script—strip PHI, replace variable slots with placeholders, but keep length and tokenization behavior identical.
00:02:50 Dana: For warmup, what's best practice? We see big variance if we don't warm the KV cache.
00:03:05 Marta: Two-phase runs: cold start run (no priming) then warm run where the cache is primed with top-k prefixes from the trace. Track hit-rate and latency delta.

00:03:30 Jordan: On KV cache measurement: capture per-request cache_hit boolean, cache_key length, and hit latency. Report hit-rate by bucket: short prompts (<128 tokens), medium (128-512), long (>512).
00:03:55 Carlos: Could you walk through an example where cache helps throughput but hurts cold-start fairness?
00:04:10 Jordan: Sure. If you have heavy repeated prefixes from a triage prompt, cache reduces token generation for that cohort. But initial requests suffer until primed. For multi-tenant, we need LRU or segmented caches to avoid eviction noise.
00:04:40 Priya: Segmented caches meaning per-org or per-user namespaces?
00:04:50 Marta: Per-namespace makes more sense for tenant isolation; we also measure cross-tenant contamination in the benchmark. We'll give config templates for namespace sizes.

00:05:10 Samira: Batching — we propose three policies to test: minimal batching (priority to latency), fixed-time batching (e.g., 20ms aggregate window), and throughput-first batching (batch until fill or 50ms). Measure latency SLO break rate at each.
00:05:35 Evan: Also measure variance of cost per token since batching changes GPU utilization. We'll model cost-per-token under each policy with your request mix.
00:05:50 Rashid: Quantization — we're nervous about hallucinations with 4-bit. How do we catch degradations reliably?
00:06:05 Jordan: Two-layer approach: automated eval suite that measures exact-match/F1 on known QA prompts and a human-in-the-loop small eval for nuanced outputs. Also use embedding-based similarity and semantic drift metrics.
00:06:30 Priya: Are quantized models deterministic? Small differences in tokenization cause big downstream changes.
00:06:40 Marta: Quantization adds numerical noise but determinism depends more on RNG seeds and beam/search settings. We'll lock sampling to greedy/top-k as needed for comparison. Also run multiple seeds and report variance.

00:07:10 Liam: For VPC/on-prem, network latency matters. How should we factor regional differences?
00:07:25 Jordan: Run network latency sensitivity by injecting artificial RTT between app and model nodes. Capture p95 delta per 10ms RTT step. Also test intra-VPC private endpoints vs cross-region fallbacks.
00:07:45 Dana: For on-prem GPU density, do you have guidance on benchmark hardware configs?
00:07:55 Samira: We'll provide candidate configs: single A10x8 equivalent pool, multi-node A100 pool, and a CPU-fallback baseline. But we recommend testing with your planned instance types; we'll map them to our kernel/runtime flavors.

00:08:20 Carlos: About apples-to-apples: we have license constraints, some models are larger or use different tokenizer. How do you normalize?
00:08:35 Jordan: Normalize by controlled configuration: same context length, same sampling settings, same prompt canonicalization. For tokenizer differences, we compare at byte-level tokenization where possible or run tokenized length normalization so compute is comparable. We'll also include per-token preprocessing cost in total latency.
00:08:55 Priya: Can we include an embargoed competitor run? We've talked to another vendor but need side-by-side numbers for our internal comms.
00:09:10 Samira: We can accept competitor-run artifacts, but we need provenance. Also we won't publish competitor data; it's for your internal evaluation.

00:09:30 Jordan: Load generation details: recommend two modes — trace-replay mode and synthetic-mode. Trace-replay replays captured request intervals and payloads. Synthetic mode recreates statistical properties: inter-arrival distribution (poisson or bursty pareto), length distributions, user session semantics (think: multi-call conversational sessions).
00:09:55 Dana: For session semantics, we have many chat sessions with incremental context growth. How to simulate that?
00:10:10 Marta: Build a session driver that replays sequences of messages with realistic think-time between user messages. The KV cache priming should be done per session so you can observe cache warm-up within a session context.

00:10:40 Rashid: Metrics storage — where do we aggregate traces?
00:10:50 Jordan: We'll ship a local collector that writes to S3 or your HDFS; the collector tags events with run-id, seed, and system config. We'll also include a small dashboard bundle for plotting p50/p95/p99, GPU util, and cache hit-rate over time.

00:11:10 Carlos: Ok show us a quick example config?
00:11:15 Marta: (screen share) Here's a sample harness run.yaml: model: redwood-llama-13b-8bit, batching_policy: fixed-20ms, kv: enabled, kv_namespace: zenith-test, load_profile: zenith-trace-48h, concurrency: 50. You'll see warmup_phase: 10m, run_phase: 30m, cooldown: 5m.

00:12:00 Jordan: Important: the warmup phase must mirror production arrival patterns otherwise the KV cache and kernels aren't representative. So if your production has bursty traffic at 3pm every day, include a burst phase in the warmup.

00:12:35 Priya: For the run durations, should we do multiple replicates?
00:12:45 Samira: Yes, at least 3 replicates per config. We'll run with different seeds and compute mean and standard deviation. Also capture GPU-side metrics for variance.

00:13:10 Liam: Regarding audit logs and KMS—if we run against a private deployment with HSM, does Redwood need key access?
00:13:25 Samira: Redwood's private agent can be deployed with customer-managed KMS; we don't hold keys. For audit logs, we can ship aggregated telemetry without PII. We'll include the secure deployment checklist.

00:13:50 Rashid: A few quick nitty-gritty: tokenization mismatch caused earlier baseline to look better for vendor X. How do we prevent that?
00:14:05 Jordan: For fairness, we do two passes: canonicalized prompt pass and raw prompt pass. The canonicalized pass controls for tokenization differences; the raw pass shows real-world behavior. We report both.

00:14:30 Carlos: When you say report cost, how granular? We want per-request, per-token, and monthly extrapolation given our traffic.
00:14:45 Evan: We'll provide per-run cost breakdown: infra (GPU), network egress, storage IO for KV, and amortized license fees. Then project monthly costs using your 95th-percentile concurrency and expected sustained qps.

00:15:10 Priya: Cache eviction policy experiments — can we test LFU vs LRU?
00:15:20 Marta: Yes, we'll include LFU, LRU, and segmented LRU configs. For each, we record hit-rate by namespace and by prompt-shape.

00:15:40 Jordan: Another practical note: tokenization differences affect token count which affects batching efficiency. We'll include a tokenization step that records token counts per prompt for each model.

00:16:05 Rashid: For quality monitoring with quantization, you mentioned embedding-based drift. Can you elaborate?
00:16:15 Jordan: Compute embedding of model output and reference output, then measure cosine similarity. Use a threshold tuned on your eval set to flag potential regressions. Combine with pass/fail heuristics on golden prompts.

00:16:40 Carlos: What about repeatability — do you save model checkpoints or exact docker image + weights for the run?
00:16:50 Samira: Absolutely. Each run artifacts bundle includes model identifier (hash), runtime kernel version, container image digest, and hardware topology. That way runs are reproducible.

00:17:10 Dana: Network shaping — can we emulate VPN overhead?
00:17:20 Jordan: Yes, our loadgen can inject per-connection overhead and encrypt/decrypt latencies. For VPC setups we'll test with traffic routed through your gateway appliance to measure realistic overhead.

00:17:45 Priya: How do you handle model warm caches when comparing two different model sizes? The larger model might have different KV entry sizes.
00:17:55 Marta: We normalize by measuring cache storage footprint and hit-rate per token. For large models that store bigger KV entries, we report hit-rate per storage byte so you can see cost-effectiveness.

00:18:15 Jordan: Let's go through an example benchmark plan for Zenith: Phase 1: Data prep and prompt sanitization + share trace. Phase 2: Baseline runs (unquantized model, minimal batching), Phase 3: Quantized runs and batching experiments, Phase 4: KV cache configs and multi-tenant tests, Phase 5: VPC on-prem sensitivity and final report.

00:18:50 Carlos: Timeline? We want pilot decision by mid-August.
00:18:55 Samira: If we get traces by next week, we can complete phases 1–3 by 2025-08-05 and phases 4–5 by 2025-08-18. That aligns with mid-August decision.

00:19:15 Priya: A few more edge cases: truncated context when token budget exceeded. Do we simulate policy for truncation?
00:19:30 Jordan: We'll implement configurable truncation policies (head, tail, summarize) and measure quality drop per policy. We'll include a recommended policy for clinical prompts (prefer head-truncation with summary fallback).

00:19:55 Rashid: Are there plans to test model fallbacks (e.g., route to smaller model on load)?
00:20:05 Marta: Yes, we'll include routing policy experiments: latency-first fallback vs cost-first fallback, and measure user-perceived latency under overload scenarios.

00:20:25 Dana: About SLOs — what should we define? p95 < 300ms for 90% of requests? That seems optimistic for long sequences.
00:20:40 Jordan: Agree. We recommend SLOs tied to cohort: short prompts p95 < 200ms, medium p95 < 400ms, long p95 < 1s. These are placeholders we can tune with your team.

00:20:55 Carlos: Anything else on instrumentation?
00:21:05 Evan: We'll add distributed tracing headers and token-level timestamps in the trace. That lets you attribute latency to decode step, kv lookup, and kernel execution.

00:21:30 Samira: Ok let's open for quick Q&A and then recap next steps.

00:21:40 Liam: Quick security note—our auditors will need proof that audit logs are tamper-evident. Can Redwood support append-only logs with signed hashes?
00:21:55 Samira: Yes, our private deployment can configure WORM-style logging and sign log batches. We'll add that to the security checklist.

00:22:10 Priya: One last: can we run a smoke test inside our VPC before handing over full data traces?
00:22:20 Jordan: Absolutely. We'll run a small smoke harness that uses synthetic prompts derived from your histogram. That reduces risk and speeds iteration.

00:22:35 Samira: Recap of next steps: Samira to share harness repo + security checklist; Priya to upload trace sample; Jordan to draft KV/batching configs; set follow-up run planning call week of 7/28.

00:22:55 Carlos: Great thanks everyone. This was super helpful.
